newsitem.title: FRANCE: France stresses hands-off policy on Algeria.
newsitem.headline: France stresses hands-off policy on Algeria.

text.p: The French government reasserted its hands-off attitude towards Algeria on Thursday, saying it had no business meddling in the internal affairs of its violence-torn former North African colony.
"Algeria is not France. That must be understood and admitted once and for all. It is a sovereign country," Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told the weekly L'Express.
"It is up to Algeria to solve its problems, up to the Algerian people to decide their destiny," he said.

Ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, head of the National Assembly's Foreign Affairs Committee, summed up France's policy after de Charette briefed a special closed-door session of the panel on Algeria as "neither intervention nor interference".
He stressed that Paris, which suffered a wave of bombings in 1995 blamed on Algerian rebels and faces threats of fresh attacks, wanted to be in step with its European Union partners.
"France has no business undertaking an isolated action...It must keep its policy within a European and Euro-Mediterranean approach with its partners," Giscard d'Estaing said.

An estimated 60,000 people have been killed since Algeria plunged into civil strife after the authorities cancelled 1992 elections that the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) was poised to win. Violence has flared during the current Ramadan Moslem fast.
Both Charette and Giscard d'Estaing welcomed President Liamine Zeroual's pledge to hold parliamentary elections soon.
The Foreign Ministry quoted de Charette as telling the closed-door hearing that France hoped the poll would be held in full openness and all legal political groups would take part.
While de Charette pointedly refused to tell L'Express if Algiers should negotiate with Moslem fundamentalist rebels, Giscard d'Estaing said they must be allowed to run in the poll.

"All political groups, including Islamists, must be allowed to field candidates, and all leaders, except those who are personally involved in terrorist attacks, must be able to take part in the election campaign," he said.
His statement was condemned as "a blatant interference" by former anti-Islamist Algerian presidential candidate Said Sadi.
"France claims it refrains from any interference but it is interfering all the time...The FIS cannot be brought into a democratic process," Sadi told French radio Beur-FM.
Algerian envoy to France, Hocine Djoudi, told the daily Le Parisien that the election date would be announced soon but the outlawed FIS would not be allowed to run.
The French government this week rejected a call from the Socialist opposition to take the lead in shaking Europe out of silence on Algeria.

European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier told parliament on Wednesday that France had repeatedly called for genuine dialogue and reconciliation as the condition for restoring peace but that depended entirely on the Algerians.
"This does not mean an embarrassed silence or indifference on our part, but merely the recognition that (Algeria) is a sovereign state," he said.

President Jacques Chirac has ruled out cutting off aid to France's former colony despite threats by Algerian guerrillas who accuse Paris of propping up Zeroual. He said last month that isolating Algeria economically would cause chaos.
